In [[statistics]], and especially in the statistical analysis of [[psychology|psychological]] data, the '''counternull''' is a statistic used to aid the understanding and presentation of research results. It revolves around the [[effect size]], which is the mean magnitude of some effect divided by the [[standard deviation]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Pashler, Harold E. |author2=Stevens, S. S. |title=Steven's handbook of experimental psychology |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |location=Chichester |year=2002 |pages= 138, 422 |isbn=0-471-44333-6 | quote = The counternull revolves around an increasingly common measure called “effect size,” which, essentially, is the mean magnitude of some effect (e.g., the mean difference between two conditions) divided by the standard deviation (generally pooled over the conditions).}}</ref>

The '''counternull value''' is the effect size that is just as well supported by the data as the [[null hypothesis]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Rubin, Donald B. |author2=Rosenthal, Robert |author3=Rosnow, Ralph L. |title=Contrasts and effect sizes in behavioral research: a correlational approach |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK |year=2000 |pages= 5 |isbn=0-521-65258-8 }}</ref> In particular, when results are drawn from a distribution that is symmetrical about its mean, the counternull value is exactly twice the observed effect size.

The null hypothesis is a [[Statistical hypothesis testing|hypothesis]] set up to be tested against an alternative. Thus the counternull is an alternative hypothesis that, when used to replace the null hypothesis, generates the same [[p-value]] as had the original null hypothesis of “no difference.”<ref>{{cite journal
 | author = Iacobucci, Dawn
 | author-link = Dawn Iacobucci
 | year = 2005
 | title = From the Editor
 | journal = [[Journal of Consumer Research]]
 | volume = 32
 | pages = 6–11
 | doi = 10.1086/430648
 | url = http://wiscinfo.doit.wisc.edu/jcr/PDFs/p-values.pdf
 | accessdate = 2007-08-01
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20051108183721/http://wiscinfo.doit.wisc.edu/jcr/PDFs/p-values.pdf
 | archive-date = 2005-11-08
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref>

Some researchers contend that reporting the counternull, in addition to the ''p''-value, serves to counter two common errors of judgment:<ref name=Rosenthal1994>{{cite journal
 | author = Rosenthal, R.
 |author2=Rubin, D.B.
 | year = 1994
 | title = The counternull value of an effect size: A new statistic
 | journal = [[Psychological Science (journal)|Psychological Science]]
 | volume = 5
 | issue = 6
 | pages = 329–334
 | doi = 10.1111/j.1467-9280.1994.tb00281.x
 | url =http://pss.sagepub.com/content/5/6/329 
 | doi-access = 
 | url-access = subscription
 }}</ref>
* assuming that failure to reject the null hypothesis at the chosen level of statistical significance means that the observed size of the "effect" is zero; and
* assuming that rejection of the null hypothesis at a particular ''p''-value means that the measured "effect" is not only statistically significant, but also scientifically important.
These arbitrary statistical thresholds create a discontinuity, causing unnecessary confusion and artificial [[controversy]].<ref>Pasher (2002), p. 348: "The reject/fail-to-reject <nowiki>[the null hypothesis]</nowiki> dichotomy keeps the field awash in confusion and artificial controversy."</ref>

Other researchers prefer [[confidence interval]]s as a means of countering these common errors.<ref>
{{cite journal| title= Review of ''Contrasts and Effect Sizes in Behavioral Research: A Correlational Approach'' by Robert Rosenthal, Ralph L. Rosnow & Donald B. Rubin
 | first= Robert J.| last=Boik | journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association 
 | volume=96 | year= 2001| pages=1528–1529
 | quote=If interval estimates of standardized effect size measures are desired, then a more sensible approach is to construct confidence intervals having fixed confidence coefficients.| issue= 456 | jstor=3085927| doi= 10.1198/jasa.2001.s432}}</ref>
